lines.text: Why does lightning seek the ground?
Lightning doesn't seek the ground. Most bolts never even touch it.
And the flash you see falling? It's actually going up.
Inside the storm, updrafts slam ice crystals into soft hail. Every hit swaps a little charge.
Light crystals rise with the plus. Heavy hail keeps the minus. The cloud splits into layers.
The negative layer pushes the ground's electrons away, leaving a positive shadow that follows the storm.
Between them, a hundred million volts. And still the air holds. Breaking it takes a stronger field than we've ever measured in a cloud. How lightning starts is still an open question.
What comes down first isn't the bolt. It's a faint channel, jumping about fifty meters at a time, branching blindly toward wherever the field is a bit stronger.
A few dozen meters up, the field below spikes. Sparks climb from trees, lampposts, blades of grass.
One touches the leader. Only that decides where it strikes.
The circuit closes, and now it goes up: a wave of charge racing to the cloud at a third of light speed.
Thirty thousand amps. Thirty thousand degrees. Five times the Sun's surface, in a channel two centimeters wide.
The channel stays hot. New leaders dash down it, and new flashes rise, three or four in under half a second. That's the flicker.
The air turns to plasma and blasts outward. That shockwave is thunder: three seconds per kilometer.
Most lightning stays inside the cloud, jumping between layers far closer than the ground. Some goes cloud to cloud, or fades in midair.
Of those that hit, nine in ten carry negative charge. The rest drop from the anvil, over ten kilometers out, under clear sky. Rare, but blamed for many wildfires.
From towers and peaks, some even start at the bottom and climb.
A lightning rod doesn't attract lightning. It just makes sure that last jump comes from grounded metal, not your roof.
And yes, it strikes twice. The Empire State Building takes about two dozen a year.
No bolt seeks the ground. It gropes blindly, and in the last few meters, the ground rises to meet it.
